[quote=oceanice_republics;60198561][u][b]The Last Day of the Republic[/b][/u]

[spoiler= Oceanice Coup]The hallways of the Gate of Berlienwerk ran long and quiet, its ceilings vaulted high with iron pennants and stained frescoes of forgotten triumphs. The air was thick, nearly mournful.
President Vanklyis Herman passed slowly along the Sergal Guards at the doors. Their halberds gleamed in the lamplight, and they gazed directly ahead. He gave a curt wave of his hand.

"Go away."

The guards halted, tightly holding their gleaming weapons, then bowed their heads and departed. The echo of their boots traveled down the corridor until silence reigned once more.
Vanklyis stepped into his office. The office was large but oppressively bare, its walls covered in shelves of heavy books, decrees, and state documents. The massive desk in the middle was piled high with bills, petitions, and legislation, all awaiting his acceptance or denial. He sat down in the chair with a soft groan, the weight of both his years and his office bearing into his back.

He began to leaf through the paperwork mechanically, trade adjustments, military appropriations, judicial rulings, each signature laid with the same cold precision. His pen scraped against parchment, the only sound filling the room.

And then he spotted it.

A red envelope out of place among the government-gray stacks. No seal of the Republic, no insignia of the ministries. Just his name, handwritten in sharp ink.
Curious, he broke the wax and unfolded the letter.

The handwriting was rushed, angled. Luma's voice sprang to life on the page.

It was not the official language, not a polished script. It was raw. It spoke of the terror she had endured, the massacres of the town, the screams at night, the endless march of soldiers who burned homes to ash. It spoke of his name spoken with dread among the young, of how he had become a shadow figure, a tyrant whose hands dripped with the grief of a thousand families.

"You are not feared. You are hated. You are not remembered as a leader. You will be remembered as a terror."

The President stiffened. His hand shook a little, the paper rustling in his grasp.

A sudden look of anger appeared on his face, but underneath, something colder was there as he realized something. A mirror reflected him in his last moments.
Beyond the official, muted disputes erupted. Secretaries, generals, and officials spoke in hushed tones in the marble hallways.

Within, Vanklyis breathed shallowly. His eyes scanned the letter once more, this time more slowly, as though every word was extremely weighty. The quiet tick of the ornate clock on the shelf grew louder by the second.

Abruptly, his chest constricted. The hand clasping the desk turned ice-white, knuckles rigid as the propped pen fell from his other hand. Papers flew, the red letter fluttering to the floor like blood spreading on marble.

His body spasmed against the chair. He attempted to cry out, but there was no sound. His eyesight blurred, constricting into tunnels of darkness.
Outside, the ministers were still arguing

oblivious, or refusing to go in. Fear paralyzed them. The President of the Republic was solitary. The final thing his eyes settled on, before the darkness dragged him down, was Luma's writing, the red ink spreading across the page. And the bells of Berlienwerk started to ring far off, heralding an end none of them yet dared to utter.

[u][b]The Burial of Vanklyis Herman[/b][/u]

Berlienwerk Capital, Three Days Later
The Grand Rotunda of the Berlienwerk Gate was hung in black and silver drapery. Massive banners of the Republic hung listlessly over the pillars, the people's faces gazing up silently. President Vanklyis Herman's coffin rested in the middle, guarded by Sergal and Human Guards in ceremonial steel. His face had been smoothed out for viewing, although the heaviness of bitterness remained in every crease.

Crowds stood at the plaza edges outside, experiencing varied emotions. There were those who were genuinely sad, and others who whispered in muted relief. Priests, generals, and ministers circulated like vultures in suits, all bowing at the coffin, but each already contemplating the political repercussions.
The formal eulogy was delivered in a wooden tone by the Minister of State, but it was not warm. The words "hero," "builder," "father of the Republic" rang out against the marble, empty and strained. Few believed them.

And then the whispers began. Behind the curtains, in the antechambers of the Rotunda, the Council of Officials was already gathering. The black uniforms of the generals conflicted with the shiny coats of the ministers. The smell of incense blended with sweat and fear.

"The Republic cannot be without a leader," General Kravos said, pounding his fist on the table. His chest was covered in medals, and his eyes were as sharp as a hawk. "The army has to take over until everything is stable again."

Ridiculous," Minister Drosvek spat, his jowls trembling. "A general with his boots on the constitution? You will reduce us to a junta!

"And what would you turn us into?" Kravos sneered. "A bunch of office drones drowning in paper?"

The arguments escalated. Voices tangled, chairs scraped against the floor, and shouts of betrayal and incompetence rang throughout the chamber.

The Treasury Chief muttered to another minister, "If Kravos seizes power, we'll all be hanged. Better we join Drosvek.

Others whispered the contrary, however: "The army has the guns. Best not to be on the wrong side of them. In the meantime, the Sergal Guard Commander stood silently against the wall, ears lowered, observing. Loyalty to the Guard was to the Republic, not to warriors. Yet even they understood that a decision would have to be made shortly.

At one point, two ministers almost got into a fight. Papers were scattered from the table, and a chair fell over. The quarrel got so heated that the mournful sound of the funeral hymn outside could hardly be heard.

Suddenly, the chamber doors burst open. A junior aide rushed in, pale as chalk.

The crowd. the crowd out there is chanting.
"Chanting what?" Drosvek growled.

The aide swallowed hard.

They chant for a new republic. They say the old one died with Herman.

The room froze. Ministers looked at each other, fear and opportunity tangling in their eyes.

The coffin outside was still. The people were mournful and spoke in hushed tones. The flags of the Republic fluttered slightly as though they sensed a wind. Within, a tough fight went on.

[u][b]The Coup Against the Semi-Authoritarian Republic[/b][/u]

The death of Vanklyis Herman left a power vacuum that the Semi-Authoritarian Republic could not contain. Without a power figure to bring fear, order, and power left dislove and truth about the government within their Authoritarian secrecy rule.

Minister Drosvek moved swiftly, declaring himself Acting Head of the Republic. His voice crackled through state radio, broadcast, and news.
"To keep things stable, the Council trusts me. There will be order. The Republic goes on."

But his words fell flat. For the first time in generations, humans and furries alike stood side by side, their disdain for the semi-authoritarian government uniting them. A rumbling discontent with the present government had circulated in whispers of bringing to an end the long-standing regime that had a legacy of oppression and autocratic rule.

Crowds paraded through the capital. Torn Republican flags with black stripes were waved by people. Sergals and Canines carried hand-made signs reading "No More Terror!" and "The People's Republic is Dead!"

Initially, they marched in protest. Later the soldiers followed them. Armored troop carriers, commanded to clear the streets, rolled instead towards Berlienwerk Square. Soldiers jumped off, not to confront the people, but to stand with them. The chants become louder.

"DOWN WITH THE REGIME!"
"OUR VOICE, OUR RIGHT!"
"FREEDOM FOR THE PEOPLE!"

Drosvek and his supporters stood on the balconies of the Gate, looking down upon the throng of citizens and troops. His face was pale, and his cheeks hung sweating.
General Kravos struck the railing with his palm.

Crush them now! Before it is too late!

But it was already too late. Units of Sergal Guards, once the most loyal defenders of the Republic, were breaking off, saluting the crowd rather than the Council.

There was gunfire in the plaza. Defectors battled loyalist units. Molotovs exploded against armored vehicles, sending smoke curling into the air. Berlienwerk's steps, polished just days earlier for the funeral, now streamed with blood and flames.

Internally, the Council Chamber grew extremely rowdy. There were calls for discussions from some of the ministers and cries for martial law from others. Some fled through side corridors. One was dragged back by furious soldiers who had turned against them.

Amidst the storm, the crowd burst through the gates. Humans and furries alike assaulted the large doors of Berlienwerk, their slogans echoing off the marble halls where laws had once been silently signed. Portraits of Herman were torn off walls. Banners of the Republic were burned.

Drosvek attempted to speak to the chamber once more, banging his fist *
"I am the authority of this Republic!"

But the roar outside drowned him. The thunder of boots and voices swept closer, until the doors burst inward and the chamber was flooded with soldiers and citizens alike.
The ministers cowered. Drosveks papers were scattered across the floor.

And for the first time since its establishment, the power of the Oceanice Republic was in the hands of the people and not the state.

The Sergal Guard silently dipped their halberds, not to a president, nor a council, but to the marchers' will. The bells of Berlienwerk tolled once more outside, no longer in mourning, but in revolution.
The marble corridors of the Berlienwerk Gate were echoing with shots. Chandeliers were shrouded in smoke and dust as the final defenders of the Republic prepared to die where their President had reigned.

The Hardliner Conservatives rallied under Minister Drosvek, their rhetoric now stripped to raw survival. The Republic lives only if we break them here! he screamed, his voice echoing down the corridor. Few believed him, but none dared desert now.

The Special Delta Spears, commandos in black, held the stairwells with machine guns. They were aware that the people were surging outside; their rifles clattered in disciplined bursts, mowing down those who attempted to rush up the front steps.

On the roof, the White Seal Special OPS took positions with sniper rifles and heavy launchers, their pale camo blending into the marble spires. From above, they rained down fire on the masses gathering in the plaza. Molotov flames licked the statues below, but still the White Seals fired, precision sharp, their faces set like stone.

The Secret Sereckist donned black armor and masked visors. They operated in small teams, knives and silent guns at the ready for the corridors. They softly made vows to their slain President, promising to slay a hundred before they themselves were apprehended.

The plaza outside was in disarray. Furries and people surged forward with makeshift barriers, rifles they had stolen, and appropriated vehicles. Soldiers who had defected rolled a commandeered tank up to the gates. The initial assault occurred at dusk. The western gate collapsed beneath the blast of the tank. The Delta Spears returned fire, bringing many down, but more just kept on coming. Rebels poured in, yelling, firing, and hurling firebombs. The large murals of Berlienwerk shattered as bullets streaked across them.

On the east stairs, Sergal Guards fought their former comrades. Some battled hard to the last, halberds swinging in arcs, claws slick with blood. Others threw down their arms and merged with the crowd, 
The Council Chamber became a fortress. Drosvek stood there, ringed by his final circle of loyalists, the walls sandbagged, the windows barred with overturned desks. Behind him, the Sereckists waited with serpents, blades drawn, pistols loaded.

The chamber doors were struck by explosions. The individuals were within. There was gunfire on the marble. The hardliners dropped one by one, Drosvek's ministers dragged from their hiding places, their shrieks masked by the tempest outdoors.

The White Seals made their last stand in the grand stairwell, rifles spitting fire until they were overwhelmed. The Delta Spears fought room by room, their black uniforms turning red as they bought seconds with their lives. The Sereckist Enforce slit throats in the dark, then vanished into the smoke, striking again like phantoms, before finally being dragged down in the bloodied corridors.
Finally, the doors to the Council Chamber flew open. Drosvek was on his own now, his papers strewn about, his voice trembling as he cried out above the din.

You'll ruin the Republic! You'll bring nothing but anarchy!
A furry rebel raised the torn flag high.
No. The Republic destroyed itself.

The room went quiet as Drosvek was dragged from his podium, his voice consumed by the wails of the populace. The fight was finished. The final loyalists were dead on the marble. The Gate of Berlienwerk, seat of iron rule, had become the grave of the regime. The sun burst through smoke-choked heavens outside as the mob poured into the plaza. The Semi-Authoritarian Republic had ended.

[u][b]The Aftermath[/b][/u]

Smoke still billowed from the shattered windows of the Gate of Berlienwerk, swirling into the night air like the dying gasp of some beast. The marble plaza, polished for parades and speeches, was now smeared in soot, the blood, and shattered glass. Burned flags of the old Republic were trampled in the mud, trodden underfoot by the boots of those who had brought it to its end.

The dead had not yet been counted. Streets were lined with makeshift stretchers, volunteers carrying the wounded past toppled barricades. Mothers wept beside their children. Defectors in uniform embraced civilians as brothers. The price of freedom hung heavy in the air.

Within the devastated halls, the Council Chamber was a cemetery of silence. Papers still rustled where bullets had perforated the ceiling. The formerly gilded murals of Herman's "triumphs" were charred and cracked, the faces of the regime's idols shattered to dust. Nothing but echoes were left of the final stand.

And still, in the square, there was a stirring. Humans and furries alike stood together, voices hoarse but unbroken. From among them was raised the shredded flag of the Republic, repainted with new colors. There was a cheer, not of victory, but of release, the sound of chains being broken. What remained of the Semi-Authoritarian Republic was gone. But so too were thousands of lives after fighting 5 days to take within the last stand of the capital building.[/i][/spoiler]

[i]From the moment the coup began, intelligence communities had their eyes set on livestreams from all angles, media posts about the revolt, formulating plans of actions and rushing to move things into place if any number of things happened which would need attention. In Lavia, aircraft and their crews were readied, and the whirr of jets and propellers cut through the still, warm air of the morning. The first in air were the fighters and AWACS planes, scrambled to monitor the airspace of the nation now in revolt and intercept any aircraft crossing the straight. After them, cargo planes lumbered into the air, filled with still groggy troops and their supplies which would immediately needed to stage an intervention if the situation devolved into civil war. On the sea, a battle group was receiving its orders to muster and send off, to position themselves off the coast of Oceanice and disregard the demilitarized zone that was ratified not weeks earlier.

Airstrips on Makinar, Dominic, and Liguarta became hives, with veritable swarms of planes being seen by civilians looking out their office windows to see what the racket is. Stations were put on high alert for anticipation of an incident, an action taken by either side of the revolt to engage Lavian troops, for a potential war that might require full military involvement. As Lavia learned of the beginning of the battle for Berlienwerk, those mobilized forces were finally issued orders. The cargo planes took to the air once more, now filled with paratroopers and medical supplies. As the medical carriers headed to Berlienwerk to drop supplies to the rebels via airdrop, the paratroopers headed to the islands to the south of Makinar, looking to prevent any short range missiles being used from there if some extremists decided that as their final act.[/i]
